idiom_name: struct with an embedded pthread_mutex_t and hand-written lock/unlock helpers
implementation_notes: POSIX supplies only the primitive: pthread_mutex_init/pthread_mutex_lock/pthread_mutex_trylock/pthread_mutex_unlock/pthread_mutex_destroy on a pthread_mutex_t declared inside the object's struct, with PTHREAD_MUTEX_INITIALIZER for static objects and mutex kinds (fast, recursive, error-checking) selected through attributes. C11 adds mtx_t/mtx_lock/mtx_unlock in <threads.h>, but that header is optional (__STDC_NO_THREADS__) and often absent, so pthreads is the practical default. Nothing about the pattern is provided: the object, the published lock (a pointer to the member or an accessor function), the init/destroy lifecycle and every acquire/release pair are hand-written, and the compiler will not stop a caller that skips the lock or copies the struct.
pitfalls: pthread_mutex_lock and friends are not async-signal-safe, and a 'fast' mutex self-deadlocks when the same thread locks it twice - use PTHREAD_MUTEX_RECURSIVE or an error-checking kind if re-entry is possible.

Copying the struct (assignment, memcpy into a container, passing by value) copies the mutex: undefined behaviour and two silently different critical sections; publish a pointer, never the object by value.

C has no scoped guard, so every error path must unlock; use a single-exit convention or a cleanup-attribute helper, and destroy the mutex only when it is unlocked (pthread_mutex_destroy returns EBUSY otherwise).
The published lock is only as good as its documentation: without a convention naming which mutex guards which fields and in which order they are taken, collaborators deadlock or race.
